summary: Chlorzoxazone is a centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant used as an adjunct to rest, physical therapy, and other measures for the relief of discomfort from acute, painful musculoskeletal conditions. It acts on the spinal cord and subcortical areas to inhibit polysynaptic reflexes. Common effects are drowsiness, dizziness, and gastrointestinal upset; urine may turn orange or purple-red. The most important serious risk is idiosyncratic, unpredictable hepatotoxicity, which can rarely be severe or fatal - patients should stop the drug and seek care at the first sign of liver injury.
indications: As an adjunct to rest, physical therapy, and other measures for the relief of discomfort associated with acute, painful musculoskeletal conditions

dosage.d: 250-500 mg three or four times daily
dosage.n: Start lower and increase as needed

dosage.d: May increase to 750 mg three or four times daily
dosage.n: Reduce to lowest effective dose as symptoms improve
Use for the shortest duration needed

admin: Take by mouth, with food or a meal if it causes stomach upset
Tablets may be crushed and mixed with food or a beverage if needed for swallowing
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest period as an adjunct to rest and physical therapy
Avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants while taking it
Stop the drug and contact a clinician at the first sign of liver problems (nausea, fatigue, dark urine, jaundice)
moa: Chlorzoxazone is a centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant. It acts primarily at the level of the spinal cord and subcortical areas of the brain, where it inhibits multisynaptic (polysynaptic) reflex arcs involved in producing and maintaining skeletal muscle spasm. The result is a reduction in muscle spasm and associated pain and limitation of movement. It does not act directly on the muscle fiber or the neuromuscular junction.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to chlorzoxazone or any component of the formulation
relative: Pre-existing liver disease or impaired hepatic function
Concurrent use of other hepatotoxic drugs or alcohol
Elderly patients (increased sensitivity to CNS effects and falls)
monitor: Symptoms and signs of hepatotoxicity (anorexia, nausea, malaise, abdominal pain, dark urine, jaundice)
Liver function tests if hepatic dysfunction is suspected

preg: The safety of chlorzoxazone in pregnancy has not been established; there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit clearly justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: It is not known whether chlorzoxazone is excreted in human milk. Caution should be exercised when administered to a breastfeeding woman.
renal: There is limited information on use in renal impairment; use with caution and monitor for accumulation of effects.
hepatic: Chlorzoxazone is associated with idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity and is extensively metabolized by the liver. Use with caution and generally avoid in patients with hepatic impairment or a history of liver disease. Discontinue immediately if signs of liver injury appear.

major: Other CNS depressants (opioids, benzodiazepines, sedative-hypnotics, alcohol) - additive sedation and respiratory/CNS depression
Other hepatotoxic drugs (e.g., acetaminophen in large doses, isoniazid) - additive risk of liver injury
moderate: CYP2E1 inhibitors or inducers (e.g., disulfiram, isoniazid, chronic alcohol) - may alter chlorzoxazone metabolism (it is a CYP2E1 probe substrate)
Monoamine oxidase inhibitors - may enhance CNS depressant effects
minor: Antihistamines and other sedating drugs - additive drowsiness
interactions.food: May be taken with food to reduce gastrointestinal upset; food does not markedly affect efficacy.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - it adds to CNS depression and increases the risk of liver injury.
interactions.diagnostics: Can cause abnormal liver function tests; metabolites may discolor the urine orange or purple-red, which can interfere with urinalysis.

common: Orange or purple-red discoloration of the urine
serious: Hepatotoxicity (idiosyncratic, can be severe or fatal)
rare: Allergic skin rash, urticaria, or redness

monitoring: Watch for early signs of hepatotoxicity (fever, rash, anorexia, nausea, fatigue, right upper quadrant pain, dark urine, jaundice)
Liver function tests if hepatic injury is suspected or in at-risk patients
Degree of sedation and ability to perform tasks requiring alertness
Symptom response to guide tapering to lowest effective dose
counsel: This medicine can make you drowsy or dizzy - do not drive or operate machinery until you know how it affects you
Do not drink alcohol while taking it, and avoid other sedating medicines
Your urine may turn orange or purplish-red; this is harmless
Stop the medicine and seek medical attention right away if you have nausea, loss of appetite, tiredness, stomach pain, dark urine, or yellowing of the skin or eyes
Use only as directed, together with rest and physical therapy, for the shortest time needed
pk: Within about 1 hour of an oral dose
Peak blood levels approximately 1-2 hours after dosing
About 3-4 hours, consistent with three- to four-times-daily dosing
Store at controlled room temperature (20-25 C); protect from moisture
pearls: Idiosyncratic, unpredictable hepatotoxicity is the key serious risk - can be severe or fatal; stop at the first sign of liver injury
Avoid in pre-existing liver disease and avoid alcohol/other hepatotoxins
Causes sedation - counsel against driving and combining with other CNS depressants
Harmless orange/purple-red discoloration of urine is common and can be mistaken for hematuria
Use as a short-term adjunct to rest and physical therapy at the lowest effective dose
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time.
overdose: Overdose can cause initial gastrointestinal upset (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) followed by drowsiness, lethargy, hypotonia, sluggish reflexes, and, with large amounts, respiratory depression, hypotension, and loss of consciousness. Management is supportive: protect the airway, provide assisted ventilation and circulatory support as needed, perform gastric decontamination (e.g., activated charcoal) if appropriate, and monitor liver function. There is no specific antidote.
